drills.q: What happens to the low twelve bits of a virtual address?
options: Nothing; they are the offset and pass through untranslated
They index the first page table level
They are checked against the page's permissions
They select a byte within a cache line
drills.why: Which is why translation happens at page granularity, and why a page is the unit of permission, residency and faulting.

drills.q: Why is the page table a four-level tree rather than one array?
options: A flat table would need 2 to the 36 entries per process
Trees are faster to search
Each level has different permissions
To support pages of different sizes
drills.why: Levels describing nothing are simply absent, which is why a process with a sparse address space costs almost nothing to describe.

options: 512 eight-byte entries is exactly one page, so every node of the tree is a page
It divides 48 evenly
It matches the cache line size
It is the widest index the hardware can decode
drills.why: Allocating a level costs the same as allocating anything else, which is what makes the sparse case cheap.

drills.q: What does a TLB miss cost?
options: A walk of the tree, up to four dependent loads, each of which may miss in cache
One extra cycle
A trap into the kernel
A disk access
drills.why: And it appears in no instruction count, which is why it is invisible unless you look for it.

drills.q: Roughly how much memory does a typical TLB cover with 4 KB pages?
options: A few megabytes
A few hundred kilobytes
A few gigabytes
All of physical memory
drills.why: A few thousand entries at 4 KB each. Working sets larger than that miss regularly, which is the entire argument for huge pages.

drills.q: What does asking for a gigabyte of memory consume?
options: Nothing; it reserves addresses with no physical pages behind them
A gigabyte
A gigabyte of swap
A page table large enough to describe it
drills.why: The memory appears on first touch, one fault per page, which is why allocating a gigabyte costs nothing and touching it costs 262144 faults.

drills.q: Why is the first pass over a freshly allocated array slower than the second?
options: Every page is being faulted in for the first time
The cache is cold
The prefetcher has not learned the stride
The allocator is still zeroing it
drills.why: Both cache and prefetcher effects exist too, and the fault is the larger one and the one that appears in no instruction count. A benchmark that skips the warm-up measures the fault handler.

drills.q: A program maps a hundred gigabyte file and reads two pages. What is its resident set?
options: Eight kilobytes
A hundred gigabytes
Two pages plus the page tables to describe the mapping
Undefined until the pages are written
drills.why: Virtual size and resident set can differ by orders of magnitude and both are correct, which is why memory profilers disagree with each other and with the operating system.

options: The kernel promising more memory than it has, since allocation is lazy
Allocating more than the process requested, for alignment
Reserving swap in advance of use
Mapping the same page into several processes
drills.why: It is why forking a large process succeeds and why an allocation almost never fails: the failure was deferred to the moment a page is touched, where there is no way to report it.

drills.q: Why does the OOM killer exist?
options: The failure was deferred past the point where it could be returned to the caller
To reclaim memory from processes that leak
To enforce per-process limits
To free swap space
drills.why: Turning overcommit off makes allocations fail honestly and makes a great deal of ordinary software stop working, which is why almost nobody does.

drills.q: What is the difference between a minor and a major fault?
options: Minor means the page is in memory somewhere; major means it must be read from storage
Minor means read-only, major means write
Minor is handled in hardware, major in the kernel
Minor is for anonymous memory, major for file mappings
drills.why: High minor counts mean the program is touching new memory, which may be fine. High major counts mean it is waiting for storage, which almost never is.

drills.q: Two processes map the same file shared. What do they see?
options: Each other's writes, with no system call involved
Private copies, from copy on write
The same bytes until either writes, then copies
Undefined behaviour
drills.why: It is the fastest inter-process communication there is, and a private mapping is the copy-on-write case instead.

drills.q: What enforces that .rodata cannot be written?
options: Permission bits in the page table entry, checked in the same lookup that translates
The linker, which rejects writes at build time
The allocator, which refuses to hand out that range
A guard page around the section
drills.why: The linker recorded the intent and the loader set the bits, and the check costs nothing because it happens inside a lookup that was going to happen anyway.

drills.q: Which page can be evicted without writing anything?
options: A clean page backed by a file
Any clean page
Any page that has not been accessed recently
A page belonging to a process that is not running
drills.why: Anonymous memory has nothing on disk holding its contents, clean or not, so even an untouched anonymous page has to go to swap. That is why swapping costs a write where dropping page cache costs nothing.

drills.q: What is swap actually good for?
options: Evicting pages that were allocated and never used again, freeing space for page cache
Extending memory beyond what was installed
Making large allocations succeed
Holding memory for suspended processes
drills.why: A working set larger than physical memory means constant major faults and a system that appears to have stopped. A machine swapping steadily is not using extra memory, it is dying slowly.
